outline.rationale: The user is new to ML but wants conceptual scaffolding to read RLHF papers, so the outline front-loads the prerequisite concepts those papers assume (language models, fine-tuning, RL vocabulary) before walking through the RLHF pipeline itself. Node 1 establishes motivation (the alignment problem) since papers assume you know why RLHF exists. Nodes 2-3 build the two foundations RLHF sits on—LM training and RL terminology—kept separate because they're genuinely distinct prerequisite domains. Nodes 4-5 cover the two technically novel pieces (reward modeling from preferences, policy optimization), which are the heart of the papers. Node 6 synthesizes them into the canonical three-stage pipeline. Node 7 covers reward hacking/KL penalties, a recurring theme in the literature that papers spend real space on. Node 8 directly serves the stated goal of reading key papers. I deliberately excluded math/code detail, hyperparameters, and hands-on training mechanics per the confirmed understanding. Nodes are MECE: motivation, two prerequisites, two mechanisms, synthesis, pitfalls, and a reading guide have low content overlap.
